files.codex/u1-answer-key.json:
{
  "body": "Looking at Cells (lesson): strong reports include magnification for each observation and a size estimate. Onion epidermal cells: rectangular, in rows, visible cell wall, a nucleus that stains darker with iodine, no chloroplasts (the bulb grows underground). Cheek cells: irregular, rounded or flat, a dark-staining nucleus, a thin membrane, no cell wall. Typical estimates: onion cells about 100 to 300 micrometers long; cheek cells about 50 to 70 micrometers across. Analysis: the cell wall gives plant cells a fixed, boxy shape; the absence of chloroplasts in onion is because those cells do not photosynthesize. Accept any reasonable estimate that is supported by a stated field-of-view diameter.

The Naked Egg: Osmosis Lab (assignment): a strong hypothesis names the direction of water movement and gives the reason (water moves toward the higher solute concentration). Method holds constant: egg size, volume of solution, time, temperature, blotting before weighing. Expected results: distilled water, mass increases (about +10 to +20%); 10% salt, mass decreases a little (about -3 to -8%); corn syrup, mass decreases sharply (about -20 to -30%). Corn syrup and salt water are hypertonic to the egg; distilled water is hypotonic. Evidence for "hypertonic": the egg lost mass, so water moved out. Percent change lets eggs of different starting mass be compared.

Cells and Transport Check (assessment):
1. Mitochondrion. It releases energy from glucose and stores it in ATP (cellular respiration).
2. Cell wall and chloroplasts (a large central vacuole is also accepted as typical of plant cells).
3. The cell membrane is made of a phospholipid bilayer: small nonpolar molecules (oxygen, carbon dioxide) slip between the lipids; ions and large polar molecules (glucose) need protein channels or carriers. That is what selectively permeable means.
4. a) Water moves into the red blood cell; it swells and may burst (lyse), because pure water is hypotonic and an animal cell has no wall. b) Water leaves the plant cell; the membrane pulls away from the wall (plasmolysis) and the plant wilts. c) No net change; the solution is isotonic.
5. Diffusion and osmosis move substances down a concentration gradient and need no energy from the cell. Active transport moves substances against the gradient and requires ATP; example: the sodium-potassium pump, or root cells taking up mineral ions from soil.
6. 1 cm cube: surface area 6 square cm, volume 1 cubic cm, ratio 6:1. 2 cm cube: 24 square cm, 8 cubic cm, ratio 3:1. The smaller cube has more membrane per unit of volume, so materials reach every part faster. That is why cells stay small and large organisms are made of many cells.
7. Percent changes: A +12.0%, B -4.0%, C -18.0%. Solution A was hypotonic (water moved in). Solution C had the highest solute concentration (largest loss). Claim, evidence and reasoning must use the numbers.
8. Salt on the slug's moist skin makes the outside strongly hypertonic, so water leaves its cells by osmosis faster than it can be replaced. A strong answer names osmosis, the gradient, and the direction of water movement.
Scoring tip: on "Uses evidence", a student who calculates correctly but never says which way water moved and why is Developing; the reason (toward higher solute concentration) is what earns Proficient.",
  "id": "u1-answer-key",
  "purpose": "answer-key",
  "title": "Answer key: Cells and Transport",
  "visibility": "teacher-only"
}
files.codex/u1-overview.json:
{
  "body": "How do things get into a cell?

Every living thing is made of cells, and every cell is wrapped in a cell membrane. The membrane is selectively permeable: it lets some substances through and keeps others out. That one property keeps you alive. Your cells take in oxygen and glucose, push out carbon dioxide and wastes, and hold on to the proteins and DNA they need.

Three ways across the membrane:
- Diffusion: particles spread from where they are more concentrated to where they are less concentrated. No energy is needed.
- Osmosis: the diffusion of water across a membrane. Water moves toward the side with more dissolved solute.
- Active transport: the cell spends energy (ATP) to pump particles against their concentration gradient, from low to high.

Key words: organelle, nucleus, mitochondrion, chloroplast, ribosome, cell wall, solute, concentration gradient, hypertonic, hypotonic, isotonic.

In this unit you will look at real cells under a microscope, then use a shell-less egg as a model cell to watch osmosis happen. By the end you should be able to predict what happens to any cell placed in any solution, and explain why.",
  "id": "u1-overview",
  "purpose": "context",
  "title": "Crossing the Membrane",
  "visibility": "students"
}
files.codex/u1-teacher-guide.json:
{
  "body": "OBJECTIVES
- Students follow a multistep microscope procedure to prepare wet mounts and record observations with magnification and scale (RST.9-10.3).
- Students design and carry out a controlled osmosis investigation, organize measurements in a data table and calculate percent change (RST.9-10.3, RST.9-10.7).
- Students use precise terms (selectively permeable, hypertonic, hypotonic, isotonic, active transport) to explain how materials cross the membrane (RST.9-10.4).
- Students explain the central idea of a text or data set about cell transport and support it with specific details (RST.9-10.2).

MATERIALS
- Compound light microscopes, slides, cover slips, droppers, iodine stain, onion, toothpicks for cheek cells (or prepared cheek-cell slides), Elodea leaves if available
- For the egg lab, per group: three raw eggs soaked 24 to 48 hours in white vinegar until the shell dissolves (start this two days ahead), distilled water, 10% salt solution, light corn syrup, three 400 mL beakers or cups, a balance reading to 0.1 g, paper towels, labels
- Goggles and gloves; closed-toe shoes on lab days
- Chart paper for a class data table

FIVE-DAY PLAN
Day 1: Read Crossing the Membrane together. Quick-draw: students sketch what they think a cell looks like, then compare their sketches with a plant and an animal cell diagram. Introduce the organelles by job (nucleus: instructions; mitochondrion: releases energy as ATP; ribosome: builds proteins; chloroplast: captures light; cell wall: support). Start the eggs soaking in vinegar.
Day 2: Lesson activity: Looking at Cells. Students prepare onion and cheek wet mounts, find each at 40x, 100x and 400x, and estimate cell size from the field of view. Debrief: which structures did you see in one and not the other, and why?
Day 3: Demonstrate diffusion with a drop of food coloring in still water and a dialysis-tubing bag of starch in iodine water (or describe it). Model osmosis with the gummy-bear question: which way will water move? Groups plan the egg lab: hypothesis, variables, constants. Eggs go into their solutions at the end of class.
Day 4: Weigh the eggs after 24 hours and complete The Naked Egg: Osmosis Lab data table. Groups add results to the class table and calculate percent change. Discuss the red blood cell in pure water and a wilting lettuce leaf in salad dressing. Introduce active transport with the sodium-potassium pump.
Day 5: Assessment: Cells and Transport Check (one class period, no AI help). Students who finish early start the lab report analysis paragraph.

DIFFERENTIATION
- Support: provide a labeled cell diagram and a three-column organizer (structure, job, plant/animal/both). For the lab, give a partly filled data table and the percent-change formula with one worked example: (final mass - starting mass) / starting mass x 100.
- Support: pair students for microscope work so one focuses while the other records; let students photograph the field of view through the eyepiece.
- Extension: have students graph percent change against solute concentration using a fourth egg in 5% salt, and estimate the concentration at which the egg would neither gain nor lose mass (the isotonic point).
- Extension: research how kidney dialysis or IV saline uses the same ideas, and explain why hospitals never give pure water by IV.
- Multilingual learners (ELL): build a word wall with the prefixes hyper- (above, more), hypo- (below, less) and iso- (equal) and their cognates (Spanish hiper-, hipo-, iso-). Accept lab analyses that use sentence frames: "The solution was ___ to the egg, so water moved ___ the egg by osmosis."
- Safety: no eating or tasting in the lab; wash hands after handling raw eggs; dispose of eggs in a sealed bag.

FAMILY NOTE
This week in Biology we are studying cells and how materials move into and out of them. Your student will look at onion and cheek cells under a microscope and use an egg with its shell dissolved in vinegar as a model cell to watch osmosis, the movement of water across a membrane. Ask your student to predict what would happen to a raisin left in a glass of water overnight, and why. Lab days need closed-toe shoes.",
  "id": "u1-teacher-guide",
  "purpose": "context",
  "title": "Teacher guide: Cells and Transport",
  "visibility": "teacher-only"
}
files.codex/u2-answer-key.json:
{
  "body": "Coin-Toss Genetics (lesson): heads = B, tails = b on each parent's coin. Expected proportions: BB 25%, Bb 50%, bb 25%; dominant phenotype 75%. With 10 tosses, results often stray far from the expected (for example 4 BB, 3 Bb, 3 bb); with 100 tosses or the pooled class total, results should be close to 25:50:25. A strong analysis says the 1:2:1 model is consistent with the data when the deviations are small relative to the sample size, and explains that each toss is independent and that chance variation averages out in larger samples (the law of large numbers).

Punnett Square Practice (assignment):
1. Pp x Pp gives PP, Pp, Pp, pp: 1/4 of the offspring are expected to be white (pp).
2. Bb x bb gives Bb, Bb, bb, bb: genotypes 1 Bb : 1 bb; phenotypes 1 brown : 1 white.
3. Tt x Tt. A 3:1 ratio (75 tall : 25 short) appears only when both parents are heterozygous; the short plants (tt) must have received a t from each parent, and both parents are tall, so each is Tt.

Pedigree Detective (assignment):
1. The trait is recessive: two unaffected parents (Carlos and Ana) have an affected daughter, so both must carry the allele. Carlos Aa, Ana Aa, their daughter aa.
2. Their unaffected son is AA or Aa; the probability he is a carrier is 2/3 (of the three unaffected outcomes AA, Aa, Aa, two are carriers).
3. Red x white snapdragons: all pink (RW). Pink x pink: 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white.
4. Roan is codominance: both red and white hairs appear. Roan x roan: 1 red : 2 roan : 1 white.
5. Mother IAi, father IBi: possible children IAIB (AB), IAi (A), IBi (B), ii (O), each with probability 1/4.
6. Mother carrier XBXb, father XBY: daughters all have normal color vision (half are carriers); sons have a 1/2 chance of red-green color blindness. A son gets his X from his mother.
7. The pedigree must show three generations, correct symbols, shading for affected individuals and a genotype under each person. Accept any equivalent layout.

Heredity Check (assessment):
1. Genotype: the alleles an organism has (Ff). Phenotype: the observable trait (freckles). Homozygous: two identical alleles (FF or ff). Heterozygous: two different alleles (Ff).
2. Ff x ff: 1/2 Ff (freckles), 1/2 ff (no freckles). Probability of no freckles = 1/2.
3. No. Each child is an independent event; the probability for the fourth child is still 1/4.
4. RrYy x RrYy: 9 round yellow : 3 round green : 3 wrinkled yellow : 1 wrinkled green. Wrinkled green = 1/4 x 1/4 = 1/16.
5. The father cannot be the man with type AB blood: a type O child is ii and must receive an i from each parent, and an AB parent has no i allele. Either of the other two men could be the father, so blood type alone cannot identify him.
6. Hemophilia is X-linked recessive. A son receives his only X from his mother; a carrier mother passes the allele to half her sons, who have no second X to mask it. Daughters need two copies, one from each parent, which is much rarer.
7. Expected: 3/4 x 200 = 150 dominant, 50 recessive. 142 : 58 is close to the 3:1 model; small deviations are expected by chance. A strong answer says the data are consistent with the model and that a larger sample would test it more strongly.
Scoring tip: give credit for correct reasoning in a Punnett square even when an arithmetic slip changes the final fraction; the criterion "Correct Punnett squares" is about the setup.",
  "id": "u2-answer-key",
  "purpose": "answer-key",
  "title": "Answer key: Heredity",
  "visibility": "teacher-only"
}
files.codex/u2-overview.json:
{
  "body": "Predicting offspring

Why do some children have a parent's eye color and others a grandparent's? About 160 years ago, a monk named Gregor Mendel answered part of that question by crossing pea plants and counting thousands of offspring.

Each parent passes on one allele (version) of each gene. An organism's two alleles are its genotype; the trait you can observe is its phenotype. A dominant allele (B) shows its trait even when only one copy is present; a recessive allele (b) shows only when there are two copies (bb).

A Punnett square shows every combination of alleles the offspring could receive. For two heterozygous parents (Bb x Bb):

        B     b
  B    BB    Bb
  b    Bb    bb

That gives genotypes in a 1 BB : 2 Bb : 1 bb ratio, and a 3 : 1 ratio of dominant to recessive phenotypes.

A Punnett square gives probabilities, not guarantees. Each offspring is a new coin toss. In this unit you will test that idea with real coin tosses, practice crosses, read family pedigrees, and meet traits that do not follow the simple dominant-recessive pattern.",
  "id": "u2-overview",
  "purpose": "context",
  "title": "Punnett Squares",
  "visibility": "students"
}
files.codex/u2-teacher-guide.json:
{
  "body": "OBJECTIVES
- Students use a simulation to decide whether results from a cross are consistent with the 1:2:1 model, and explain why larger samples come closer to predicted ratios (HSS.IC.A.2, RST.9-10.3).
- Students use Punnett squares to predict genotype and phenotype ratios, treating each possible offspring as an outcome in a sample space (HSS.CP.A.1, RST.9-10.4).
- Students translate a family history written in words into a pedigree chart and use it to infer genotypes (RST.9-10.7).
- Students apply the multiplication rule for independent events to a dihybrid cross (HSS.CP.A.2).

MATERIALS
- Two coins per pair (or two-sided counters marked B and b), tape to label the coins
- Graph paper or a spreadsheet for the class data table
- Pedigree symbol key (squares for males, circles for females, shaded for affected, a horizontal line for parents, a vertical line to children)
- Optional: pictures of snapdragons (incomplete dominance) and roan cattle (codominance)

FIVE-DAY PLAN
Day 1: Read Punnett Squares together. Introduce vocabulary with a quick sort (allele, genotype, phenotype, homozygous, heterozygous, dominant, recessive). Model a Pp x Pp cross for flower color. Ask: if a pair of Pp plants has four seeds, must exactly one be white?
Day 2: Lesson activity: Coin-Toss Genetics. Pairs simulate 10, then 40, then 100 offspring of a Bb x Bb cross. Pool the class data and compare the class total with the pairs' totals. Discuss sample size.
Day 3: Assignment: Punnett Square Practice. Work through problem 1 together, then students work in pairs. Exit ticket: what does the 3:1 ratio mean in problem 3?
Day 4: Beyond simple dominance: incomplete dominance, codominance, multiple alleles (ABO blood types) and X-linked traits. Model one pedigree from words. Students begin Pedigree Detective.
Day 5: Assessment: Heredity Check (one class period, no AI help). Students who finish early may complete Pedigree Detective.

DIFFERENTIATION
- Support: provide blank 2x2 and 4x4 Punnett square templates and a step list (write each parent's genotype, split the alleles of each parent along the edges, fill each box, count). Let students build crosses with letter tiles before writing them.
- Support: for pedigrees, give the symbol key on a card and draw the first generation together.
- Extension: have students derive the 9:3:3:1 ratio for a dihybrid cross both with a 16-box square and with the multiplication rule (3/4 x 3/4 = 9/16), then use a chi-square test on the class coin data.
- Extension: research one human trait often wrongly taught as a simple single-gene trait (for example eye color) and explain why it does not follow a 3:1 pattern.
- Multilingual learners (ELL): pair each term with a picture and a short example (heterozygous = two different letters, Bb). Many terms have cognates: dominante, recesivo, genotipo, fenotipo, probabilidad. Accept answers that use frames such as "The probability of ___ is ___ because ___ of the 4 boxes show ___."

FAMILY NOTE
This week your student is learning how traits are passed from parents to children, using Punnett squares and coin-toss simulations. A good question to ask at home: if two parents each carry one hidden (recessive) allele for a trait, what is the chance that their child shows the trait? (One in four, and that chance is the same for every child.) Your student will also learn how to read a family tree, called a pedigree. No family information is needed or collected for this assignment.",
  "id": "u2-teacher-guide",
  "purpose": "context",
  "title": "Teacher guide: Heredity",
  "visibility": "teacher-only"
}
files.codex/u3-answer-key.json:
{
  "body": "Floating Leaf Disks (lesson): disks under the lamp float steadily over 10 to 20 minutes; disks closer to the light float sooner (lower ET50); disks in the dark stay sunk. Strong analyses explain that photosynthesis produces oxygen, which collects in the spaces inside the leaf and makes the disk buoyant, so the rate of floating is a measure of the rate of photosynthesis. Bicarbonate supplies carbon dioxide. Light intensity is the independent variable, number of floating disks over time the dependent variable, and the dark cup is the control. Limitations: disk size, leaf age, the heat of the lamp.

Yeast at Work (assignment): balloon circumference increases fastest at about 37 degrees C, slower at 25, very little at 10, and little or none at 50 (high heat damages the yeast's enzymes). The graph should plot temperature on the x-axis and circumference after a fixed time on the y-axis. Strong answers say the relationship is not linear: it rises to an optimum and then falls. Carbon dioxide inflates the balloon; it is produced by the yeast's respiration and fermentation as it breaks down sugar. Bottles must have the same amounts of yeast, sugar and water.

Follow a Carbon Atom (assignment): a strong essay follows one carbon atom in order: carbon dioxide in the air enters a leaf through a stoma; in the chloroplast, photosynthesis uses light energy to build it into glucose; the plant stores it in starch or uses it in its own respiration; an animal eats the plant and digests the starch to glucose; the glucose travels in the blood to a muscle cell; in a mitochondrion, cellular respiration breaks the glucose down and the carbon leaves as carbon dioxide, carrying no usable energy, while the released energy is stored in ATP; the animal exhales the carbon dioxide and the cycle can begin again. It distinguishes the path of matter (carbon) from the flow of energy (light to chemical energy to ATP to heat), and uses both equations accurately. Citations should come from the reading.

Cell Energy Check (assessment):
1. Photosynthesis: reactants carbon dioxide and water (plus light energy); products glucose and oxygen; in chloroplasts. Respiration: reactants glucose and oxygen; products carbon dioxide, water and ATP; in mitochondria (glycolysis begins in the cytoplasm).
2. Plants respire too: every living plant cell needs ATP, including root cells and all cells at night, so plant cells have mitochondria as well as chloroplasts.
3. ATP is the molecule that stores energy in a form cells can spend. When a cell breaks the bond to its last phosphate (ATP to ADP), energy is released to power work such as active transport (Unit 1) and muscle contraction.
4. Aerobic respiration uses oxygen and yields about 30 to 32 ATP per glucose (older textbooks give 36 to 38). Fermentation needs no oxygen and yields 2 ATP per glucose. Examples of fermentation: yeast making bread rise (alcoholic fermentation) and muscle cells during hard exercise (lactic acid fermentation).
5. ET50 values: 10 cm, 8 min; 20 cm, 12 min; 30 cm, 19 min. The closer the lamp, the faster half the disks floated, so the rate of photosynthesis increases with light intensity. The dark control shows that light is needed; without it no disks floated, so the floating is caused by photosynthesis, not by time alone.
6. Accept: the oxygen in the room came from photosynthesis (released by the splitting of water); the carbon dioxide we exhale came from glucose broken down in our mitochondria; the glucose came from photosynthesis. Strong answers connect the two equations as a cycle of matter, with energy flowing through rather than cycling.
7. The mouse's air would run out of oxygen, or fill with carbon dioxide, without the plant; with the plant in the light, the plant's photosynthesis replaces oxygen and removes carbon dioxide, and the mouse's respiration supplies the plant with carbon dioxide. In the dark, the plant only respires, so the mouse would not survive as long.
Scoring tip: on "Process explanations", a student who memorized the equations but says plants do photosynthesis instead of respiration is Developing; plants do both.",
  "id": "u3-answer-key",
  "purpose": "answer-key",
  "title": "Answer key: Cell Energy",
  "visibility": "teacher-only"
}
files.codex/u3-overview.json:
{
  "body": "Every cell needs a steady supply of energy, and almost all of it starts as sunlight.

Photosynthesis happens in chloroplasts. Plants, algae and some bacteria use light energy to build sugar from carbon dioxide and water, and release oxygen:
6 CO2 + 6 H2O + light energy -> C6H12O6 (glucose) + 6 O2

Cellular respiration happens in the mitochondria of nearly every cell, plant and animal alike. It releases the energy stored in glucose and stores it in ATP, the molecule cells spend to do work:
C6H12O6 + 6 O2 -> 6 CO2 + 6 H2O + energy (stored in ATP)

Notice that each equation is the other one run backward. The oxygen you breathe out of the air was released by photosynthesis, and the carbon dioxide you breathe out is the raw material a plant builds with.

When there is no oxygen, some cells switch to fermentation. It releases far less energy per glucose, but it keeps a cell going for a while. Yeast fermenting sugar is what makes bread rise.

Remember Unit 1: the mitochondrion was the organelle that makes most of a cell's ATP. This unit opens it up. You will measure photosynthesis in floating leaf disks, measure respiration in yeast, and follow a single carbon atom through the living world.",
  "id": "u3-overview",
  "purpose": "context",
  "title": "Energy In, Energy Out",
  "visibility": "students"
}
files.codex/u3-teacher-guide.json:
{
  "body": "OBJECTIVES
- Students follow a multistep procedure to measure the rate of photosynthesis in leaf disks and of respiration in yeast, recording measurements with units (RST.9-10.3).
- Students graph experimental data on two quantitative variables and describe the relationship (HSS.ID.B.6, RST.9-10.7).
- Students trace and explain the complex process by which carbon and energy move between photosynthesis and cellular respiration, in an informative text (RST.9-10.2, WHST.9-10.2).
- Students define and correctly use reactant, product, ATP, chloroplast, mitochondrion, aerobic, anaerobic and fermentation (RST.9-10.4).

MATERIALS
- Leaf disk lab, per group: fresh spinach leaves, a single-hole punch, a 10 mL plastic syringe with no needle, 0.2% sodium bicarbonate solution (about 1/8 teaspoon baking soda in 300 mL water) with one drop of dish soap, two clear cups, a lamp with an LED bulb, a ruler or meter stick, a timer
- Yeast lab, per group: dry baker's yeast, sugar, four identical small bottles, four balloons, warm water at four temperatures (about 10, 25, 37 and 50 degrees C) in water baths, thermometers, string and rulers to measure balloon circumference
- Optional: bromothymol blue and a straw for a demonstration of carbon dioxide in exhaled breath (teacher only; students must not inhale)
- Graph paper or a spreadsheet

FIVE-DAY PLAN
Day 1: Read Energy In, Energy Out. Balance the two equations together and mark reactants and products in two colors. Ask: where does the mass of a tree come from? Collect predictions, then reveal that most of it comes from carbon dioxide in the air.
Day 2: Lesson activity: Floating Leaf Disks. Groups punch 10 disks, remove the air with the syringe so the disks sink, then count floating disks every minute under the lamp at two distances, with a control cup in the dark. Introduce ET50, the time for half the disks to float.
Day 3: Inside the mitochondrion: glycolysis, the Krebs cycle and the electron transport chain at the level of inputs and outputs. Compare aerobic respiration with fermentation. Set up the Yeast at Work lab; balloons are measured at 5, 10, 15 and 20 minutes.
Day 4: Finish the yeast data and graphs. Introduce Follow a Carbon Atom with a class model on the board, then students draft.
Day 5: Assessment: Cell Energy Check (one class period, no AI help). Follow a Carbon Atom is due later in the week.

DIFFERENTIATION
- Support: give a partly completed comparison chart (photosynthesis and respiration: where, reactants, products, energy in or out) and a graph frame with labeled axes. For the leaf disk lab, assign one student to count and one to record.
- Support: provide a carbon-path organizer for the writing task (air, leaf, sugar, food, muscle cell, air) with one sentence frame per step.
- Extension: have students design a third leaf disk condition (light color, bicarbonate concentration or temperature) and predict its ET50 before testing. Ask why the disks float (oxygen produced by photosynthesis collects in the leaf tissue).
- Extension: research why yeast stops fermenting at high temperature, linking to enzymes and protein shape.
- Multilingual learners (ELL): build a bilingual glossary of the equation terms. Cognates help: fotosintesis, respiracion celular, mitocondria, cloroplasto, glucosa, oxigeno. Let students explain the cycle orally or with a labeled diagram before writing, and accept writing that uses frames such as "First, the carbon atom ___. Then ___."
- Safety: the lamp gets hot; keep water away from the cord. Do not use water above 50 degrees C.

FAMILY NOTE
This week your student is learning how plants capture energy from sunlight (photosynthesis) and how every living cell releases that energy (cellular respiration). In class we are measuring photosynthesis in spinach leaf disks and respiration in yeast, the same yeast that makes bread rise. A good dinner-table question: where does the mass of a tree come from, the soil, the water or the air? Ask your student to explain the surprising answer.",
  "id": "u3-teacher-guide",
  "purpose": "context",
  "title": "Teacher guide: Cell Energy",
  "visibility": "teacher-only"
}
files.codex/u4-answer-key.json:
{
  "body": "Strawberry DNA Extraction (lesson): mashing breaks open the cell walls; dish soap dissolves the lipid membranes (cell membrane and nuclear membrane), releasing DNA; salt helps the DNA strands clump by shielding their negative charges; filtering removes cell debris; DNA does not dissolve in cold alcohol, so it comes out of solution as white, stringy, cloudy material at the boundary between the layers. We see it because millions of strands clump together. Strawberries are good because their cells have many copies of each chromosome (they are octoploid). A strong analysis connects each step to a cell structure from Unit 1.

Transcription and Translation Practice (assignment):
1. TAC GGC AAT.
2. mRNA AUG CCU GAA UAA; protein Met-Pro-Glu (stop).
3. mRNA AUG UUU GGC ACC UGA; protein Met-Phe-Gly-Thr (stop).
4. GGC to GGA still codes Gly: a silent mutation; the protein is unchanged, because the code is redundant.
5. New template TAC TAA ACC GTG GAC T; mRNA AUG AUU UGG CAC CUG (A left over); protein Met-Ile-Trp-His-Leu. Every codon after the insertion changes, and the stop codon is lost: a frameshift.
6. A substitution changes at most one codon and so at most one amino acid (and sometimes none). An insertion or deletion of one base shifts the reading frame, so every codon after it is read wrongly, usually producing a completely different, nonfunctional protein or an early stop.
7. 146 x 3 = 438 bases code for the amino acids; with a stop codon, 441.

From One Letter to a Disease (assignment): a strong essay explains, level by level: DNA: in the HBB gene, codon 6 changes from GAG to GTG (A to T substitution); mRNA: GAG becomes GUG; protein: glutamic acid becomes valine at position 6 of beta-globin (missense); molecule: when oxygen is low, sickle hemoglobin molecules stick together into long fibers; cell: red blood cells become stiff and crescent-shaped, block small blood vessels and break down early; body: pain crises, anemia, organ damage, stroke risk; inheritance: autosomal recessive, so carriers (sickle cell trait) have one normal allele and are usually healthy (link to Unit 2); population: carriers are partly protected from severe malaria, which explains why the allele is common where malaria is or was common (preview of Unit 5). It cites the reading accurately.

DNA and Proteins Check (assessment):
1. DNA: A-T, G-C. DNA template to RNA: A-U, T-A, G-C, C-G. Differences: DNA is double-stranded, RNA usually single-stranded; DNA has deoxyribose, RNA ribose; DNA uses thymine, RNA uracil. Also accept: DNA stays in the nucleus, mRNA travels to the ribosome.
2. Semiconservative: each new DNA molecule has one original strand and one newly built strand, because each original strand serves as the template for a new partner. Original strand TAGGC: new partner ATCCG.
3. mRNA AUG GUA CCC AAA UAG; protein Met-Val-Pro-Lys (stop).
4. CAT to CTT changes the mRNA codon GUA to GAA: valine becomes glutamic acid, a missense mutation. It may change how the protein folds and works, depending on where the amino acid is.
5. Every body cell has the same DNA, but each type of cell expresses (transcribes and translates) a different set of genes. Muscle cells express genes for contractile proteins; nerve cells express genes for neurotransmitter proteins.
6. Order: the gene's DNA is unzipped in the nucleus; mRNA is built from the template strand; mRNA leaves the nucleus; a ribosome binds the mRNA at AUG; tRNAs with matching anticodons bring amino acids; amino acids are joined by peptide bonds; the ribosome reaches a stop codon and releases the chain, which folds into a protein.
7. A = T = 30%, so A + T = 60%; G + C = 40%, and G = C = 20%.
Scoring tip: when a student transcribes correctly but translates from the DNA rather than the mRNA, mark "Decoding" Developing and show where the step went wrong; the reasoning is usually sound.",
  "id": "u4-answer-key",
  "purpose": "answer-key",
  "title": "Answer key: DNA and Proteins",
  "visibility": "teacher-only"
}
files.codex/u4-overview.json:
{
  "body": "In Unit 2 you predicted traits with Punnett squares, but we never asked what an allele actually is. This unit answers that question.

A gene is a stretch of DNA that holds the instructions for one protein. DNA is a double helix: two strands twisted around each other, held together by pairs of bases. A always pairs with T, and G always pairs with C. Because each strand fits the other, a cell can copy its DNA by unzipping it and building a new partner for each strand.

Proteins do most of the work in your body: enzymes, hemoglobin, muscle fibers, antibodies. Making one takes two steps:
1. Transcription (in the nucleus): a gene's DNA is copied into a messenger RNA (mRNA).
2. Translation (at a ribosome, the organelle from Unit 1): the ribosome reads the mRNA three bases at a time. Each three-base codon calls for one amino acid, and the chain of amino acids folds into a protein.

DNA -> RNA -> protein -> trait.

Different alleles are different versions of a gene's base sequence. A change in the sequence, called a mutation, can change the protein, and that can change a trait. You will extract DNA from strawberries, decode genes into proteins, and explain how one changed base causes sickle cell disease.",
  "id": "u4-overview",
  "purpose": "context",
  "title": "From Code to Character",
  "visibility": "students"
}
files.codex/u4-teacher-guide.json:
{
  "body": "OBJECTIVES
- Students follow a multistep procedure to extract DNA and explain the purpose of each step (RST.9-10.3).
- Students use the symbols and terms of molecular genetics (base pairs, codon, anticodon, mRNA, amino acid) to transcribe and translate genes and to predict the effect of mutations (RST.9-10.4).
- Students analyze the relationships among DNA, RNA, protein and trait, and the structure of the genetic code (RST.9-10.5).
- Students write an informative explanation of how a single mutation causes sickle cell disease, citing specific evidence from a text (WHST.9-10.2, RST.9-10.1).

MATERIALS
- DNA extraction, per group: 2 or 3 fresh or thawed strawberries, a zip-top bag, extraction buffer (100 mL water, 10 mL dish soap, 1.5 g salt, about 1/4 teaspoon), a coffee filter and funnel, a clear test tube or narrow cup, ice-cold 91% isopropyl or 95% ethanol alcohol (kept in a freezer), a wooden stick or paper clip hook
- A DNA model or paper base-pair cut-outs
- The Genetic Code (Selected Codons) handout, provided as a reading in the activities
- Goggles; keep alcohol away from any flame

FIVE-DAY PLAN
Day 1: Read From Code to Character. Build a short DNA model with paper bases and have students discover the pairing rule. Show how unzipping and rebuilding produces two identical molecules (semiconservative replication). Connect back: an allele is a sequence.
Day 2: Lesson activity: Strawberry DNA Extraction. Before starting, groups predict what each ingredient does. After, they explain why we can see DNA when a single molecule is far too thin to see (millions of strands clump together).
Day 3: Transcription and translation. Act it out: one student is the DNA in the nucleus, another carries the mRNA message to the ribosome, and tRNA cards bring amino acids. Practice decoding with the codon table. Start Transcription and Translation Practice.
Day 4: Mutations: substitution (silent, missense, nonsense) and insertion or deletion (frameshift). Read Sickle Cell: One Letter, Many Lives. Students plan the informative essay From One Letter to a Disease with a level-by-level organizer (DNA, mRNA, protein, cell, body, population).
Day 5: Assessment: DNA and Proteins Check (one class period, no AI help; students may use the codon table).

DIFFERENTIATION
- Support: provide a step chart (DNA template, mRNA, codons split by slashes, amino acids) and have students split every sequence into triplets before decoding. Color-code the bases.
- Support: for the essay, give the six-level organizer with the first sentence of each paragraph started.
- Extension: research how CRISPR-based gene therapy for sickle cell disease works, and explain why it targets blood stem cells rather than mature red blood cells (which have no nucleus).
- Extension: explain why the genetic code is called redundant, and why redundancy makes some substitutions harmless.
- Multilingual learners (ELL): many terms are cognates (ADN, ARN, proteina, aminoacido, mutacion, transcripcion, traduccion). Point out that transcription and translation mean what they mean in language: copying in the same language (DNA and RNA both use bases) and translating into a new one (bases into amino acids). Accept oral explanations of the extraction steps with a labeled photo sequence.
- Safety: alcohol is flammable and should stay cold and capped; wear goggles.

FAMILY NOTE
This week your student extracted real DNA from strawberries using dish soap, salt and alcohol, and is learning how the DNA code is read to build proteins. We are using sickle cell disease as an example of how a change in a single letter of DNA can change a protein and a person's health. If your student wants to try the extraction at home, all it takes is a strawberry, a sealable bag, a little dish soap, salt, water and rubbing alcohol from the freezer, with an adult nearby.

Note for teachers: some students may have sickle cell disease or trait, or family members who do. Present it as science and medicine, not as a story about any group, and avoid asking students to share their own health information.",
  "id": "u4-teacher-guide",
  "purpose": "context",
  "title": "Teacher guide: DNA and Proteins",
  "visibility": "teacher-only"
}
files.codex/u5-answer-key.json:
{
  "body": "Bead Bugs (lesson): the color that best matches the fabric should increase in number each generation, while the most visible colors decline; after three generations the camouflaged color usually makes up the largest share. A strong analysis names all four conditions in the simulation (variation: five colors; inheritance: survivors reproduce their own color; overproduction: not all bugs survive the predators; differential survival: camouflaged bugs are caught less often) and notes limitations: real organisms do not reproduce exact copies, predators learn, and selection pressures change.

Finch Beaks After the Drought (assignment):
1. Before: mean 9.4 mm, range 8.0 to 10.6 mm. Survivors: mean 9.9 mm (9.895 before rounding), range 8.6 to 10.6 mm. Percent change in mean: (9.9 - 9.4) / 9.4 x 100 = about 5.3%.
2. The center moved up and the low end of the distribution was cut off: birds with the smallest beaks became rare, and the survivors' beaks are bunched more tightly toward the deep end.
3. During the drought, the remaining seeds were mostly large and hard. Birds with deeper beaks could crack them and survive; birds with small beaks starved. This is natural selection acting on variation that already existed.
4. The offspring had deeper beaks on average than the population before the drought (mean 9.7 mm, compared with 9.4 mm). Because beak depth is strongly inherited, the change carried into the next generation, which is evolution. The offspring mean is a little lower than the survivors' 9.9 mm because beak depth also depends on other factors, such as the environment, and is not perfectly inherited.
5. No. The birds did not grow bigger beaks because they needed them; individuals do not change their inherited traits. The survivors already had deeper beaks.
6. A rainy year with plenty of small, soft seeds would favor smaller beaks, which handle small seeds more efficiently; the mean could shift back down. Selection depends on the environment, and environments change.
7. Strong answers note at least two limitations: the numbers in this data set are rounded and illustrative; we have only one island and one drought; other factors (body size, disease) could also matter; a sample of measured birds may not represent the whole population.

Did the Drug Make the Mutants? (assignment): the strongest claim is that antibiotics do not cause resistance mutations; they select resistant bacteria that already exist. Evidence: in the replica plating experiment, the resistant colonies appeared in the same positions on every copy plate, which means they were already resistant on the original plate that had never touched the drug; and resistance spreads where antibiotics are used heavily, because the drug kills the susceptible bacteria and leaves the resistant ones to multiply. The counterclaim to address: resistance appears after the drug is used, so it looks as if the drug caused it. Rebuttal: correlation in timing is not causation; the experiment separates the two. Strong essays connect to all four conditions of selection and to Unit 4 (mutations happen at random during DNA copying).

Evolution Check (assessment):
1. Variation, inheritance, overproduction (competition), and differential survival and reproduction. Example must apply each condition to one population.
2. Lamarck's idea is the inheritance of acquired traits; it is wrong because changes to an individual's body during its life do not change the DNA in its eggs or sperm. Darwinian answer: giraffes varied in neck length; those with longer necks reached more food during scarce times and left more offspring; the allele frequencies shifted over many generations.
3. Homologous: human arm and whale flipper (same bones, different functions; evidence of a shared ancestor). Analogous: bird wing and butterfly wing (same function, different structures; evolved separately in similar environments).
4. Species B. More shared sequence means a more recent common ancestor, because differences accumulate over time after two lineages split.
5. Hares whose fur matches the snow are harder for predators to see; they survive and reproduce more, so alleles for white winter fur become more common. If snow cover shrinks with a warmer climate, white hares on brown ground would be easier to see, and selection could favor brown fur or earlier color change.
6. In a population, separated groups experience different environments and different mutations; over many generations they accumulate differences; if they can no longer interbreed, they are separate species. Strong answers name geographic isolation.
7. The bead-bug data show the camouflaged green bugs rising from 20 to 26 to 33 to 39, while the red bugs fell from 20 to 12 to 7 to 4. This supports natural selection: the trait that improved survival in that environment increased in frequency.
Scoring tip: watch for "the organism adapted because it needed to". Answers that say an individual changes on purpose are Developing on "Mechanism of selection", even with correct vocabulary.",
  "id": "u5-answer-key",
  "purpose": "answer-key",
  "title": "Answer key: Evolution and Natural Selection",
  "visibility": "teacher-only"
}
files.codex/u5-overview.json:
{
  "body": "In Unit 4 you saw that mutations create new alleles. In Unit 2 you saw how alleles are passed on. Put those together with a struggle to survive, and you get the most powerful idea in biology: evolution by natural selection.

Charles Darwin and Alfred Russel Wallace described it in 1858. It needs four conditions:
1. Variation: individuals in a population differ, and much of that difference comes from different alleles.
2. Inheritance: offspring tend to resemble their parents.
3. More offspring are born than can survive, so they compete for limited resources.
4. Differential survival and reproduction: individuals with traits that suit the environment leave more offspring.

Over generations, the helpful alleles become more common. The population evolves. Individuals do not evolve; populations do. And selection does not create the traits it needs: it can only act on the variation that is already there.

Evidence that living things share common ancestors comes from many directions: the fossil record, homologous structures like the bones of a human arm, a bat wing and a whale flipper, embryos, and DNA itself, where more closely related species share more of their sequence.

In this unit you will run a predator-prey simulation, analyze finch beak data from a drought, and argue about where antibiotic resistance comes from.",
  "id": "u5-overview",
  "purpose": "context",
  "title": "Variation, Selection, Time",
  "visibility": "students"
}
files.codex/u5-teacher-guide.json:
{
  "body": "OBJECTIVES
- Students follow a multistep simulation procedure and represent changes in a population across generations (RST.9-10.3, RST.9-10.7).
- Students compare the center and spread of two data sets to describe how a population changed after a selection event (HSS.ID.A.2).
- Students write an argument from evidence about whether antibiotics cause or select resistance, and assess how well an experiment's evidence supports a claim (WHST.9-10.1, RST.9-10.8).
- Students explain the conditions for natural selection and evaluate the lines of evidence for common ancestry (RST.9-10.2).

MATERIALS
- Bead Bugs simulation, per group: a 50 cm square of patterned fabric, about 100 beads or paper dots in five colors (20 of each), one of which closely matches the fabric, a timer, cups for captured bugs
- Graph paper or a spreadsheet
- Images of homologous forelimbs (human, cat, whale, bat) and of a well-known transitional fossil series (whales or tetrapods)
- The readings provided in the activities

FIVE-DAY PLAN
Day 1: Read Variation, Selection, Time. Open with a misconception check: "A giraffe stretched its neck and passed on a longer neck. True or false?" Introduce the four conditions and the difference between acquired and inherited traits.
Day 2: Lesson activity: Bead Bugs. Groups run three generations: predators pick bugs for 15 seconds, survivors reproduce (each survivor adds one bug of its own color), and the group records counts. Pool class data and graph each color across generations.
Day 3: Evidence for evolution: homologous and analogous structures, vestigial structures, fossils, embryos and DNA comparisons. Students work through Finch Beaks After the Drought in pairs.
Day 4: Antibiotic resistance. Read Did the Drug Make the Mutants? and discuss the Lederbergs' replica plating experiment. Students outline their argument with claim, evidence, reasoning and counterclaim, and begin drafting.
Day 5: Assessment: Evolution Check (one class period, no AI help). The argument is due later in the week.

DIFFERENTIATION
- Support: provide a four-box organizer for the conditions of natural selection, with one bead-bug example in each box. Give a graph frame for bead-bug results and the formula for percent change.
- Support: for the argument, provide a claim-evidence-reasoning frame and two sentence starters for the counterclaim: "Some people think ___. However, the evidence shows ___."
- Extension: calculate allele frequencies in the bead-bug population and explain the difference between natural selection and genetic drift. Ask what would happen to a tiny population by chance alone.
- Extension: research one example of evolution observed within a human lifetime (for example, Galapagos finches, peppered moths, pesticide-resistant insects, or Italian wall lizards) and evaluate the evidence.
- Multilingual learners (ELL): use cognates (evolucion, seleccion natural, variacion, adaptacion, poblacion). Preteach the everyday and science meanings of "fitness" (being in shape vs leaving offspring) and "theory" (a guess vs a well-tested explanation). Accept a labeled comic strip of bead-bug generations as a draft of the analysis.
- Teaching note: present evolution as the well-supported science it is, and acknowledge that some students and families hold religious views on origins. Students are assessed on understanding the science, not on personal belief.

FAMILY NOTE
This week your student is studying evolution by natural selection: how populations of living things change over many generations. In class we are simulating predators and prey with colored beads and analyzing real-world patterns, such as how a drought changed a population of finches and how bacteria become resistant to antibiotics. Ask your student why doctors say not to use antibiotics for a cold (they do not work on viruses, and unnecessary use helps resistant bacteria spread).",
  "id": "u5-teacher-guide",
  "purpose": "context",
  "title": "Teacher guide: Evolution and Natural Selection",
  "visibility": "teacher-only"
}
files.codex/u6-answer-key.json:
{
  "body": "Schoolyard Quadrat Survey (lesson): density = number counted / total area sampled (for example, 38 plants in five 1 m2 quadrats = 7.6 plants per m2; in a 200 m2 area, about 1,520 plants). Random placement means every part of the area had an equal chance of being sampled, so the sample is likely to represent the whole area and the estimate is not biased by choosing where plants are easy to find. More quadrats give a more reliable estimate. Differences between sun and shade should be explained with abiotic factors (light, moisture, temperature, foot traffic). Accept any well-supported comparison.

Energy Through the Food Web (assignment):
1. Primary consumers 1,000 kcal; secondary 100 kcal; tertiary 10 kcal. About 90% at each level is used for life processes (respiration, movement, keeping warm) or lost as heat, or is never eaten or digested.
2. Because so little energy reaches the top, a fifth or sixth level would not have enough energy to support a population.
3. Snake: tertiary consumer (fourth trophic level), on grass-grasshopper-frog-snake. Hawk: secondary consumer (third level) on grass-rabbit-hawk, tertiary consumer (fourth level) on grass-grasshopper-sparrow-hawk, and quaternary consumer (fifth level) on grass-grasshopper-frog-snake-hawk. An organism that eats prey from different levels occupies more than one level.
4. Frogs decline: grasshoppers increase (fewer predators), so grass may decrease; snakes decrease (less food), and hawks may eat more rabbits and sparrows. Accept any reasoned chain that follows the arrows.
5. From plankton (0.04 ppm) to fish-eating birds (25 ppm) the concentration rises by a factor of 25 / 0.04 = 625. The chemical is stored in fat and not broken down or excreted, so each predator accumulates the amounts in all the prey it eats over its lifetime. Top predators are most at risk; DDT thinned the eggshells of birds such as ospreys, bald eagles and brown pelicans.
6. A single oak tree feeds thousands of caterpillars, so a pyramid of numbers is inverted. A pyramid of energy can never be inverted, because each level gets its energy from the level below and loses most of it.
7. Carrying capacity about 160 deer (the population levels off and fluctuates around it). Growth was fastest between years 2 and 4 (35 deer per year). Limiting factors: food, space, predators, disease, harsh winters. Near carrying capacity, births and deaths are about equal.

Wolves, Elk and Willows (assignment): there is no single correct claim; strong essays take a qualified position, such as: wolves played a real but partial role in the recovery of willows and aspen, alongside human hunting, drought, other predators and the return of beavers. Evidence for the wolf explanation: elk numbers fell sharply after reintroduction; some studies found more growth in willows and aspen after the wolves returned, especially in some places. Evidence for other explanations: elk were also hunted outside the park and eaten by growing numbers of bears and cougars; drought and winter conditions affected elk; recovery was uneven, and in many areas willows remained short because beavers, whose dams raise the water table, had not returned. Strong essays explain why the case is hard to test (no control Yellowstone without wolves) and judge the strength of each piece of evidence. They should use the term trophic cascade correctly and cite the reading.

Ecology Check (assessment):
1. Biotic: living factors (grass, deer, bacteria). Abiotic: nonliving factors (sunlight, temperature, water, soil minerals). Any two of each, correctly classified.
2. a) Mutualism (both benefit). b) Parasitism (the tick benefits, the deer is harmed). c) Commensalism (the barnacle benefits, the whale is mostly unaffected). d) Mutualism.
3. When hares are plentiful, lynx have more food and their numbers rise; more lynx eat more hares, so hares decline; then lynx starve and decline, and hares recover. The predator peak lags behind the prey peak because predators need time to reproduce after food becomes plentiful.
4. Photosynthesis removes carbon dioxide from the air and builds it into sugar (Unit 3); respiration by plants, animals and decomposers returns it; burning fossil fuels releases carbon that was stored underground for millions of years, faster than photosynthesis and the oceans can absorb it, so the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere rises.
5. Zebra mussels thrive because they have few natural predators or diseases in the Great Lakes, reproduce rapidly, and outcompete native filter feeders for plankton. Effects: less plankton for native fish larvae and mussels, clearer water, clogged water intake pipes. Strong answers connect to limiting factors and competition.
6. Density = 64 / 10 m2 = 6.4 dandelions per m2; estimate = 6.4 x 500 = 3,200 dandelions. Quadrats must be placed randomly so the sample represents the whole field.
7. Secondary succession: soil remains after the fire, so grasses and shrubs return first, then fast-growing trees, then longer-lived trees. Primary succession starts on bare rock with no soil (after a lava flow or a retreating glacier) and begins with lichens and mosses, so it is much slower.
Scoring tip: on "Energy and matter", credit the idea that energy flows and matter cycles even when the vocabulary is imperfect; the distinction is the heart of the unit.",
  "id": "u6-answer-key",
  "purpose": "answer-key",
  "title": "Answer key: Ecology",
  "visibility": "teacher-only"
}
files.codex/u6-overview.json:
{
  "body": "Ecology is the study of how living things interact with one another and with their environment. It brings together everything from this semester. The energy captured by photosynthesis (Unit 3) moves through food webs. Carbon cycles between the air and living things. Natural selection (Unit 5) shapes every species to its niche.

Levels of organization: an organism; a population (all the members of one species in an area); a community (all the populations in an area); an ecosystem (the community plus its nonliving, or abiotic, environment); the biosphere.

Energy flows. Producers capture light energy. Consumers eat producers or other consumers. At each step up a food chain, only about 10% of the energy is stored in the next level's bodies; the rest is used for life processes and lost as heat. That is why there are far fewer hawks than mice, and far fewer mice than blades of grass.

Matter cycles. Carbon, nitrogen and water are used again and again, passing between organisms, soil, water and air. Decomposers return the matter in dead things to the soil.

Populations have limits. Food, space, water, predators and disease limit how many individuals an environment can support: its carrying capacity.

In this unit you will sample a real community outdoors, calculate how energy moves through a food web, and weigh the evidence in a famous story: what happened to Yellowstone when the wolves came back.",
  "id": "u6-overview",
  "purpose": "context",
  "title": "Everything Is Connected",
  "visibility": "students"
}
files.codex/u6-teacher-guide.json:
{
  "body": "OBJECTIVES
- Students follow a sampling procedure and use data from randomly placed quadrats to estimate the size of a population, explaining why random sampling supports the inference (RST.9-10.3, HSS.IC.A.1).
- Students translate food web and energy information given in words into diagrams and pyramids, and calculate energy transfer between trophic levels (RST.9-10.7).
- Students write an argument assessing how strongly the evidence supports the claim that wolves caused a trophic cascade in Yellowstone, weighing other explanations (WHST.9-10.1, RST.9-10.8).
- Students explain central ideas about energy flow, cycles of matter and population limits, using precise ecological vocabulary (RST.9-10.2, RST.9-10.4).

MATERIALS
- Quadrat survey, per group: a 1 m square quadrat (four meter sticks or string and stakes), a random-number table or a phone random-number generator, a field guide or photo cards of common schoolyard plants, clipboards
- Graph paper or a spreadsheet
- Colored pencils for food web and pyramid diagrams
- The readings provided in the activities
- If going outdoors is not possible: a large printed "field" photo or a tray of mixed dried beans as a model community

FIVE-DAY PLAN
Day 1: Read Everything Is Connected. Sort examples into biotic and abiotic factors. Build a class food web on the board from a list of organisms and trace one path of energy and one path of carbon. Ask: what would happen if one species disappeared?
Day 2: Lesson activity: Schoolyard Quadrat Survey. Groups place five quadrats at random coordinates in a sunny area and five in a shaded area, count one chosen plant species and estimate percent cover. Back in class, calculate density and estimate the total population for each area.
Day 3: Energy pyramids, the 10% rule and biomagnification. Students work through Energy Through the Food Web. Introduce carrying capacity with a growth curve.
Day 4: Read Wolves, Elk and Willows. Run a quick structured discussion: list every piece of evidence for and against the wolf explanation. Students outline and begin drafting their argument.
Day 5: Assessment: Ecology Check (one class period, no AI help). Close the semester by asking students to name one idea from each unit that showed up in ecology.

DIFFERENTIATION
- Support: provide a data table with the density formula (count / area sampled) and a worked example; give a partly drawn energy pyramid with the producer level filled in.
- Support: for the argument, provide a two-column evidence chart (supports the wolf explanation; supports another explanation) and sentence frames for qualifying a claim: "The evidence suggests ___, but ___ also played a role."
- Extension: compare the sunny and shaded quadrats with a simple statistical test, or calculate a diversity index for each area. Research how mark-and-recapture estimates populations of animals that move.
- Extension: research another keystone species (sea otters and kelp forests, beavers and wetlands) and compare the evidence with the Yellowstone case.
- Multilingual learners (ELL): use cognates (ecosistema, poblacion, comunidad, productor, consumidor, descomponedor, energia) and a picture glossary of trophic levels. Allow students to label food webs in their home language first, then add English terms. Accept argument outlines in either language during planning.
- Outdoor work: set boundaries, check for allergies (bees, pollen), and avoid unknown plants with bare hands.

FAMILY NOTE
In this final unit of the semester, your student is studying ecology: how living things depend on each other and on their environment. We are sampling plants on the school grounds to estimate population sizes, calculating how energy moves through food webs, and examining what happened to the Yellowstone ecosystem after wolves were brought back in the 1990s. Ask your student to explain why there are so few large predators compared with plant-eaters. The answer connects to almost everything we learned this semester.",
  "id": "u6-teacher-guide",
  "purpose": "context",
  "title": "Teacher guide: Ecology",
  "visibility": "teacher-only"
}
